Continuous DNA mixture likelihood ratio (gamma model)

Source: R/gmixlr.R
gmixlr.Rd

The weight of a DNA mixture for one account of who contributed against another, from the peak heights, not only from which alleles were seen. Each account names the reference profiles it holds to be contributors (hp, the prosecution's, usually the person of interest and any undisputed contributor; hd, the defence's); the rest of the nc contributors are unknown people whose genotypes are summed over. The model's parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood under each account separately and the ratio of the two maxima reported, marker by marker and over all markers.

Usage

gmixlr(
  peaks,
  freq,
  ref = NULL,
  hp = NULL,
  nc,
  hd = NULL,
  at = 50,
  pc = 0.05,
  lambda = 0.01,
  theta = 0,
  stut = FALSE,
  deg = FALSE,
  par = NULL
)

Arguments

peaks

The peaks seen: a data frame with columns locus, allele and height, every height at least at. A marker of freq with no peak counts too (everything dropped out).

freq

The allele frequencies: a data frame with columns locus, allele and freq (above 0, summing to at most 1 at a marker; the rest is the chance of an allele not listed), and size, the fragment size in bases, needed when deg = TRUE. Every peak's allele must be listed.

ref

The reference profiles: NULL, or a data frame with columns id, locus, a1 and a2. Every profile conditions the unknowns' genotypes when theta is above 0.

hp, hd

The ids of the profiles of ref that contribute under the first and the second account (NULL: none). Contributor k of an account is its k-th named profile, then its unknowns U1, U2, ...

nc

The number of contributors: one whole number from 1 to 5.

at

The analytical threshold: one number above 0.

pc

The drop-in chance per marker: from 0, below 1.

lambda

The rate of the exponential distribution of drop-in heights above at: above 0.

theta

The coancestry coefficient: from 0, below 1.

stut, deg

TRUE to model backward stutter and degradation.

par

NULL to fit, or the parameters for both accounts: named numbers mu, omega, beta (with deg), xi (with stut) and m1, ..., m<nc> summing to 1.

Value

An object of class gmixlr, a list: lr and log10lr; fit, a data frame with one row per account (hyp, loglik the natural log likelihood at its maximum, mu, omega, beta, xi (NA when not modelled), conv (NA with par) and iter); mix, the mixture proportions (hyp, who, m); and locus, the base-10 log ratio by marker at each account's parameters.

Details

The model is the gamma model of peak heights (Cowell et al. 2015; Bleka, Storvik and Gill 2016). Contributor k has mixture proportion m_k (the proportions sum to 1) and carries 0, 1 or 2 copies n_k(a) of allele a. The height of the peak at a is gamma with shape s(a) / omega^2 and scale mu omega^2, so its mean is mu s(a) and a single heterozygous contributor's peaks have coefficient of variation omega, where s(a) = sum_k m_k n_k(a) d(a). With deg = TRUE, d(a) = beta^((size(a) - 125) / 100), degradation by fragment size in bases (beta fitted, above 0); otherwise d(a) = 1. With stut = TRUE, each allele seen passes the share xi of its signal to the position one repeat shorter (backward stutter): s(a) becomes (1 - xi) s(a) + xi s(a + 1), xi fitted. A peak lower than the analytical threshold at is not seen, with the chance the gamma gives (drop-out). A peak seen where s(a) = 0 is a drop-in, of chance pc times the allele's frequency times an exponential density of rate lambda for its height above at; a marker without drop-in has chance 1 - pc. Unknown contributors' genotypes are drawn from the frequencies with the coancestry correction theta (Balding and Nichols), given the alleles of every profile in ref; markers are independent. The alleles not seen at a marker, those of the reference profiles among them, are taken together as one allele that does not stutter and has the largest size listed at the marker; the positions one repeat below the alleles seen are kept as positions no one carries.

This is the model of EuroForMix (Bleka, Storvik and Gill 2016) with backward stutter only and its frequencies not normalised (the rest of a marker is the chance of an allele not listed), where the person of interest is a known non-contributor under hd (every profile in ref conditions the unknowns). Its tests compare the log likelihood with EuroForMix's at given parameters, which agree to 1e-6 (EuroForMix keeps its genotype weights in single precision), and the fitted maxima.

Limits, plainly. The result is only as good as the model: the number of contributors is the user's assumption, not estimated; forward and double stutter, locus-specific amplification efficiencies, peak height variance that differs by marker, and relatives among the contributors are not modelled; the frequencies are used as given (sampling error in them is ignored). Taking the alleles not seen as one allele is exact without stutter and degradation; with them, an allele not seen neither stutters nor is sized by its own fragment. Stutter needs numeric labels (repeat numbers) for the alleles seen. The fit is a numerical maximisation (BFGS over transformed parameters from several starts) and can find a local maximum; the sum over the unknowns grows as (number of genotypes)^(unknowns) per marker and is refused above 2 million combinations, so at most 5 contributors and in practice 3 unknowns. This is not a validated casework system; its likelihoods are checked against enumeration by hand and against EuroForMix, not against a laboratory's validation data. Give par to evaluate both accounts at given parameters instead of fitting them.

References

Cowell, R. G., Graversen, T., Lauritzen, S. L. and Mortera, J. (2015). Analysis of forensic DNA mixtures with artefacts. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C: Applied Statistics, 64(1), 1-48. doi:10.1111/rssc.12071

Bleka, O., Storvik, G. and Gill, P. (2016). EuroForMix: An open source software based on a continuous model to evaluate STR DNA profiles from a mixture of contributors with artefacts. Forensic Science International: Genetics, 21, 35-44. doi:10.1016/j.fsigen.2015.11.008

Balding, D. J. and Nichols, R. A. (1994). DNA profile match probability calculation: how to allow for population stratification, relatedness, database selection and single bands. Forensic Science International, 64(2-3), 125-140. doi:10.1016/0379-0738(94)90222-4

Examples

# a two-person mixture at two markers: is S a contributor, with the
# victim V, or are V and an unknown person?
peaks <- data.frame(locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), c(4, 3)),
                    allele = c(14, 15, 16, 17, 16, 17, 18),
                    height = c(1210, 380, 1150, 420, 1400, 1960, 610))
freq <- data.frame(locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), c(5, 5)),
                   allele = c(13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19),
                   freq = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.25, 0.2,
                            0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
ref <- data.frame(id = rep(c("V", "S"), each = 2),
                  locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), 2),
                  a1 = c(14, 16, 15, 17), a2 = c(16, 17, 17, 18))
gmixlr(peaks, freq, ref, hp = c("V", "S"), nc = 2, hd = "V")
#> gmixlr: 2 markers; log10 LR 1.920759, LR 83.32179
#>  hyp    loglik       mu      omega beta xi conv iter
#>   hp -43.35714 1782.500 0.09470922   NA NA TRUE    9
#>   hd -47.77985 1782.483 0.09471434   NA NA TRUE   12
#> mixture proportions:
#>  hyp who         m
#>   hp   V 0.7287494
#>   hp   S 0.2712506
#>   hd   V 0.7287524
#>   hd  U1 0.2712476
